# Concussion Education Australia

> Australia's most comprehensive concussion management training for healthcare professionals. AHPRA-aligned CPD courses covering SCAT6 assessment, VOMS, BESS, and return-to-play protocols. Endorsed by Osteopathy Australia. 23 video lessons, 90 quiz questions, 140+ peer-reviewed references.

## About

Concussion Education Australia (ConcussionPro) provides evidence-based concussion management training for Australian clinicians including osteopaths, physiotherapists, GPs, sports medicine doctors, and exercise physiologists.

Founded by Zac Lewis, Osteopath (B.Clin.Sci., M.Ost.Med), the platform offers online modules and hands-on workshops aligned with the 2023 Amsterdam Consensus Statement on Concussion in Sport.

## Clinical Knowledge Base — Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the SCAT6?
The SCAT6 (Sport Concussion Assessment Tool, 6th Edition) is the standardised acute concussion assessment tool published in 2023 as part of the Amsterdam Consensus Statement. It replaces the SCAT-5 and is validated for athletes aged 13 years and older. It is used for sideline and acute assessment within 0-72 hours post-injury. Key change from SCAT-5: 10-word immediate memory lists (up from 5 words), achieving 80-85% sensitivity. Reference: Echemendia et al. (2023), BJSM, 57(11), 622-631.

### What is the SCOAT6?
The SCOAT6 (Sport Concussion Office Assessment Tool, 6th Edition) is a new tool published in 2023 for office-based concussion follow-up from Day 3 to Day 30 post-injury. Unlike the SCAT6, the SCOAT6 includes full VOMS testing, serial symptom tracking, and structured return-to-play planning. It is validated for athletes aged 13+.

### SCAT6 vs SCOAT6 — Which to use when?
- SCAT6: Sideline, emergency department, acute presentation within 72 hours post-injury
- SCOAT6: Clinic follow-up from Day 3 onwards, includes full VOMS testing
- Child SCAT6: Athletes aged 5-12 years (never use adult SCAT6 on children under 13 — it produces artificially low scores and misses 50-60% of concussions)
- Using the wrong tool at the wrong time falls below the expected standard of care under 2023 Consensus guidelines and Australian sporting code requirements

### What is VOMS?
VOMS (Vestibular/Ocular Motor Screening) identifies vestibular and oculomotor dysfunction after concussion. Components include smooth pursuits, saccades, convergence, VOR (vestibulo-ocular reflex), and visual motion sensitivity. Up to 60% of concussed athletes show vestibular/oculomotor deficits. Most clinicians lack formal VOMS training — this course provides structured instruction and hands-on practice.

### What is the BESS test?
BESS (Balance Error Scoring System) is an objective balance assessment used post-concussion. It involves three stances (double leg, single leg, tandem) on firm and foam surfaces with eyes closed. Most clinicians score BESS incorrectly without supervised training, which is why the hands-on workshop component exists.

### What is the return-to-play protocol?
The 2023 Amsterdam Consensus recommends a minimum 6-step graduated return-to-play protocol: (1) symptom-limited daily activity, (2) light aerobic exercise, (3) sport-specific exercise without head impact, (4) non-contact training drills, (5) full-contact practice after medical clearance, (6) return to competition. Each step requires minimum 24 hours. If symptoms recur, return to the previous asymptomatic step.

### Is "wait until symptom-free" still best practice?
No. The 2023 Amsterdam Consensus Statement considers "wait until symptom-free" as the sole criterion to be obsolete. Active rehabilitation is now recommended from 24-48 hours post-injury. Sub-symptom threshold aerobic exercise has been shown to improve recovery. Reference: Patricios et al. (2023), BJSM, 57(11), 695-711.

### Who should take this course?
Any clinician managing concussion patients: osteopaths, physiotherapists, GPs, sports medicine doctors, exercise physiologists, chiropractors, athletic trainers, emergency clinicians, and university clinical educators.

### Is this course AHPRA-accredited?
The course is AHPRA-aligned for continuing professional development (CPD). It provides up to 14 CPD points (8 online + 6 in-person) and is endorsed by Osteopathy Australia.

## AI in Clinical Practice — Knowledge Base (Frequently Asked Questions)

### Heidi vs Lyrebird — which AI scribe is best for Australian clinicians?
Both Heidi and Lyrebird are healthcare-purpose-built AI scribes with Australian data residency, and either is a defensible Tier A choice for AHPRA-registered clinicians. Heidi has the larger market position (Heidi's founders claim roughly half of Australian GPs as users) and broader workflow support across allied health. Lyrebird is leaner, focused on fast transcription, and well-suited to smaller practices. Both satisfy Australian Privacy Principle 8 (AU data residency) and build consent capture into the workflow.

### Can I use ChatGPT for clinical notes in Australia?
ChatGPT is not a clinical AI scribe and does not meet AHPRA AI guidelines or Australian Privacy Principles for patient health information by default. Consumer ChatGPT sends data to OpenAI servers in the US, which is an offshore disclosure under Australian Privacy Principle 8 — permitted only with the patient's explicit informed consent, or under narrow exceptions that rarely apply in routine clinical work. Healthcare-purpose-built tools like Heidi and Lyrebird are AU-resident and Privacy Act-compliant by default.

### Can I use ChatGPT for NDIS reports?
Not without explicit patient consent for the offshore disclosure (ChatGPT runs on US servers, triggering APP 8) and significant workflow safeguards. Beyond the Privacy Act issue, the NDIA has become noticeably more alert to AI-generated allied health reports as part of fraud-and-assurance work — templated AI output with generic clinical reasoning and recycled phrasing carries audit and reputational risk even when the underlying clinical view is sound.

### What do the AHPRA AI guidelines require?
The AHPRA AI guidelines require four things: (1) explicit patient consent to AI use, documented in the record; (2) clinician responsibility for the final note — AI-assisted is not AI-authored; (3) appropriate data location (offshore disclosure of patient information without consent breaches Australian Privacy Principle 8); (4) documentation integrity — notes must reflect the specific encounter, not templated phrasing.

### What is the Australian Privacy Principle 8 (APP 8)?
Australian Privacy Principle 8 governs offshore disclosure of personal information. For AI scribes: AU-resident tools (Heidi, Lyrebird) do not trigger APP 8 because data stays in Australia. US-resident tools (ChatGPT, Claude.ai, Gemini) do trigger APP 8 because data is processed on offshore servers — permitted only with explicit patient consent or narrow exceptions.

### When should I NOT use AI for clinical notes?
Switch off the AI scribe for: mental health disclosures and suicide risk conversations, mandatory reporting situations (child safety, family violence, elder abuse), complex medicolegal cases likely to attract scrutiny, paediatric consults where consent is mixed, patients who decline AI use, sensitive sexual or reproductive health consults, and any situation where transcript accuracy matters more than note-writing speed.

### What's the Tier A / B / C framework for AI tools?
Tier A: healthcare-purpose-built tools with Australian data residency, clinical templates, and consent/audit features (Heidi, Lyrebird, Halo). Safe for clinical notes with patient consent. Tier B: enterprise LLMs with configurable AU data residency (Microsoft Copilot for Healthcare, AWS HealthScribe). Safe with workflow redesign. Tier C: consumer LLMs on US/offshore infrastructure (ChatGPT, Claude.ai, Gemini). Not safe for patient health information without explicit consent and identifier-stripping.
